title: Welcoming refugees
hookLine: the Hijra made the first Muslims migrants, and the Qur'an praises the hosts who took them in
tomorrow: why plant a tree you'll never sit under?

cards: A van pulls up outside a community center, and a family climbs out with everything they own in a few suitcases. Volunteers hold hand-lettered signs. Two of them are friends: one Muslim, one Jewish.
Ask each why she came, and both answers start in the past tense. One says: we were strangers. The other says: we were migrants.
Two old books, a memory they share, told two ways.

teach.b: The Muslim memory first. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and his companions left Mecca for Medina. That move is the Hijra.
The Qur'an describes them as people driven out from their homes and their belongings. In Medina, the Ansar, the helpers, took them in. And the Qur'an praises the hosts.

teach.h: THE ANSAR: THEY LOVE THOSE WHO FLEE.
teach.b: In Pickthall's words, they "love those who flee unto them for refuge," and they put the newcomers ahead of themselves, even when they were poor.
Some Muslims put it this way: the Hijra makes every Muslim an heir to migrants. The community's founding story is leaving home and being taken in. Now the neighbor, in its own words.
The Torah says, in the JPS translation: "Love ye therefore the stranger; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The reason is written right into the command: you were strangers too.
So both remember arriving with nothing, and both turn that memory into a duty to the person at the door. That's real common ground. And an honest difference.

The Torah's line speaks to the people who were the strangers: now love the stranger. The Qur'an's verse praises the hosts, the Ansar, who had never been migrants at all. One says: remember you were them.
The other adds: be like the ones who opened the door.

how: Many mosques and Muslim charities help newly arrived refugee families with housing, food, language and paperwork, and Muslims often recall the Hijra and the Ansar when they do; Jewish communities draw on the Torah's command to love the stranger in the same work.

o: sending aid abroad after a natural disaster
taking in people forced to leave their home
moving to another country for a better job

games.q: who's who in the welcome — tap the pairs.
p: the move from Mecca to Medina
the hosts who took them in
love the stranger: you were strangers

s: welcoming refugees is a modern cause with no roots in old scripture
the Qur'an praises the Ansar who took in those driven from home, and the Torah says love the stranger.
the Torah's line and the Qur'an's verse say exactly the same thing
both welcome. but the Torah speaks to former strangers; the Qur'an praises hosts who never were.
the Qur'an praises the people of Medina for loving those who fled to them
59:9: they love those who flee unto them for refuge.

games.q: a new family moves in across the hall. they speak a little English, and the kids look lost at the bus stop. what fits 'we were migrants'?
o: walk the kids to the bus their first week and learn the family's names.
leave a welcome card, then give them space until they've settled in.
wait for the building to set up something official for new tenants.
games.why: the Ansar didn't wait for a program. they took the newcomers in and put them ahead of themselves (59:9).

practice: Pick up one thing near you that came with you from somewhere else: a mug, a jacket, something from home. Hold it, and think of someone who arrived somewhere new with only a few things like it.
If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer; if not, just hold them in mind.

wordCard.voice: Welcoming refugees: taking in people who've had to leave home. For Muslims, the Hijra puts that story at the root.

orig.note: Arabic: the migration, the Prophet's move from Mecca to Medina. those who made it are the muhajirun.

carryVoice: Your line: we were migrants. And the hosts who opened the door are part of the story too. Take care.
